[] Ah, I think I know the one you mean — the warm brown-orange stew Lolo makes, with the peanut taste. When family makes it at home, they start with real roasted peanuts or a thick peanut butter and mix it into the sauce slowly, sometimes cooking it for a long time so the peanuts melt into a smooth, creamy texture. That’s what makes it thick.

In the store or restaurant, they might make it faster using a powder or less peanut, and sometimes they add more water to make more servings. That can make the sauce look thinner or taste different. Lolo probably also uses fresh vegetables like eggplant, long beans, and banana heart, and cooks the oxtail or beef until it’s very soft. All the flavors and oils from the meat blend with the peanuts to make the sauce rich.

Another reason is that at home, people put in extra time to stir and keep the heat just right so it doesn’t burn. In the store, they have to make a lot of food quickly, so they might not wait as long. And because Lolo makes it for family, he might taste it many times and keep adding just the right amount of peanut and seasonings, so it’s exactly how he remembers from when he was young.

So the thick peanut sauce is like a little sign: someone took their time, used real ingredients, and made it with care — just for you.

If you still want help with handling nervousness when family puts you on the spot in conversation (in any language or situation), here are some general ideas you can use:

- **Pause and breathe:** Give yourself a moment before responding. A brief pause can calm your mind and slow your heart rate.
- **Acknowledge the question:** You can say something like “Hmm, let me think” to signal you’re considering your reply — this buys you time.
- **Redirect gently:** If you’re caught off guard, you might shift the topic to something you’re more comfortable with: “That reminds me of…” or “Speaking of…”
- **Prepare phrases in advance:** Think of a few go-to responses for common topics so you have them ready when needed.
- **Use humor or lightness:** Sometimes a small joke or smile can ease the tension and help you feel more in control.
- **Set boundaries if needed:** If on-the-spot questions make you uncomfortable, it’s okay to calmly say: “I’d like to come back to that later.”

[] That’s a really good question, Mateo. Food can taste different in Baja because people there sometimes use different ingredients, cooking styles, and even water from what we have at home. In Baja California, a lot of dishes are made with super fresh seafood, homemade tortillas, and local spices. The fish, vegetables, and even the bread might come from nearby farms or from the ocean that morning, so the flavor can be new or a little different than what you’re used to.

Some cooks use special seasonings like lime, chili, or herbs that taste stronger than the ones in your favorite meals at home. Also, the air by the ocean and the way food is cooked outside — maybe on charcoal grills or in clay pots — can change how it smells and tastes. Even little things, like the temperature, how long the food travels before it’s eaten, or the kind of cheese they use, can make a big difference.

When we go to a new place, our taste buds notice all these changes, and sometimes it feels exciting, and other times it can feel… unusual. It’s okay if a new taste doesn’t feel like your favorite right away. Little by little, you might learn which parts you like most, and that can make trying new foods feel a bit more fun. And even if you don’t eat everything, noticing the colors, shapes, and smells can still be part of the adventure.
